1.s: Habakkuk asks, “How long will I cry, and you will not hear?” God answers that he is raising up the Babylonians. Habakkuk asks how a holy God can use a nation more wicked than Judah.
1.d: Habakkuk’s complaint is like the lament psalms, honest about how he felt [[bsn:Habakkuk 1:1–11]]. God seemed silent about the evil in Judah [[tosn:Habakkuk 1:2–4]], and then said he would use the Babylonians, which raised a harder question (1:13) [[tbd:002:Book of Habakkuk]]. Paul quotes 1:5 in Acts 13:41 [[bible:Acts 13:41]].

2.s: Habakkuk waits on the watchtower. God answers: write the vision plainly; it will surely come. “The righteous will live by his faith.” Woes on the oppressor follow. “The earth will be filled with the knowledge of Yahweh’s glory, as the waters cover the sea.”
2.d: “The righteous will live by his faith” is one of the Old Testament’s most important verses on faith, central to Paul and the Reformation (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11; Hebrews 10:38) [[tbd:002:Book of Habakkuk]]. The Hebrew ’emunah means steadfastness and trust, from the same root as Abram’s trust in Genesis 15:6 [[tosn:Habakkuk 2:4]].

3.s: Habakkuk’s prayer recalls God’s mighty acts, and ends: “Though the fig tree doesn’t flourish… yet I will rejoice in Yahweh… Yahweh, the Lord, is my strength.”
3.d: The prayer has musical notes, suggesting Habakkuk may have served in temple music [[tbd:002:Book of Habakkuk]]. Even if no material blessing ever came again, God is still worthy of trust and praise [[tosn:Habakkuk 3:17–19]].
